newsitem.title: TAIWAN: Taiwan proposes to host HK shipping talks.
newsitem.headline: Taiwan proposes to host HK shipping talks.

text.p: Taiwan proposed on Wednesday to host semi-official talks on shipping links with Hong Kong, which is eager to work out crucial technical issues before the British colony reverts to Chinese rule on July 1.

"We have proposed to invite Hong Kong Shipowners Association chairman George Chao to come to Taipei at the end of April to discuss future shipping links between Taiwan and Hong Kong," the semi-official Straits Exchange Foundation said.
Taiwan has officially authorised Chang Liang-jen, deputy secretary-general of the foundation, to undertake talks with Chao, Beijing's designated negotiator.

Hong Kong is the channel through which more than US$30 billion in Taiwan investments have poured into China since the late 1980s, when a political thaw unleashed an explosion of unofficial Taiwan-China ties.

Kao Koong-lian, vice chairman of the cabinet's Mainland Affairs Council, warned on Tuesday of painful consequences if no deal was reached over Taiwan's crucial shipping links with Hong Kong -- including a possible halt to bilateral sailings.
At issue is what flags should be flown on ships plying routes between Taiwan and Hong Kong.

Hong Kong's post-handover constitution states that after July 1, Hong Kong-registered ships on international routes must fly communist China's flag along with the territory's own Hong Kong Special Administrative Region flag.

Kao said Taipei would welcome ships flying the red five-star of the People's Republic of China -- but only if Beijing and Hong Kong tolerated vessels that flew the flag of the exiled Republic of China on Taiwan.

China regards Taiwan as a renegade province and refuses to recognise the Republic of China government that has ruled the Nationalist redoubt since losing the mainland in a civil war in 1949 and fleeing to the island.

To avoid the sensitive sovereignty issue, Kao said Taiwan negotiators would propose that Taiwan and Hong Kong ships lower all flags and identify themselves through telex communications before entering each other's waters.
It was not known how Hong Kong's government-in-waiting or Beijing would respond.
